items.name: Beam moving head (outdoor)
items.product: UPlight UP-B380F, 380 W IP65 beam moving head
items.what: A motorised head on a yoke, standing on a low base, that pans and tilts by remote control. It does not wash a stage with light — its lens throws one very narrow (1.8°), extremely bright shaft, like a searchlight, meant to be seen cutting through haze or smoke rather than lighting a person's face. It uses a discharge lamp, not an LED, so it needs a short warm-up when switched on. The housing is sealed and gasketed (IP65) for outdoor rigs.
items.inShow: Used to draw hard, sword-like beams through haze for concert-style looks, aerial 'beam walls' along a truss, or a single sweeping shaft — a different visual language from an even wash or a projected pattern.

needs.text: 100-240 V AC mains; draws about 500 W at full output.
DMX512 (USITT DMX512-A / ANSI E1.11), 16 channels in its one control mode.

Overhead use needs a truss clamp rated for the fixture's weight plus a secondary safety bond/cable, independent of the clamp, so a clamp failure cannot drop it — the standard entertainment-rigging practice (ICOPER, also DGUV Vorschrift 17 in Germany).

Uses a discharge lamp (350XL/380, ~2000 h life), not an LED: it needs a warm-up/cool-down cycle, and the lamp is a UV and burst hazard if the housing is opened while hot. Relamping is a technician job, not a swap done mid-show.

alternatives.why: IP66-rated, fully weatherproof hybrid beam/spot for the same outdoor slot — the benchmark 'Sharpy' beam, at a premium price.
A 280 W hybrid beam/spot/wash in a lighter body (15 kg) with much more versatility; indoor-rated only, no IP65.
A budget compact 100 W discharge beam — far cheaper and lighter, but indoor-only and noticeably less punchy at long throw.

items.name: Bee-eye matrix moving head
items.product: UPlight UP-HK1915 'Hawk Eye / Bee Eye', 19x15 W RGBW zoom moving head
items.what: A moving head whose face is not one lens but 19 small round lenses set in a honeycomb, giving it the 'insect eye' look it's named for. Each cell can carry its own colour, so the fixture can act as one wide wash, a pixel-mapped grid of separate points, or — zoomed narrow — a cluster of thin beams. Indoor use only.
items.inShow: Used for a textured, cellular wall of light, or chases and pixel patterns across the 19 cells — a different visual language from a single-lens wash or a beam moving head.

needs.text: 100-240 V AC mains, about 350 W (one listing gives 300 W).
DMX512, five modes from 21 to 97 channels depending on how much per-cell control is used.
Overhead use needs a truss clamp plus a secondary safety bond, as for any moving head (ICOPER).

items.name: Full-colour laser, 40 W
items.product: Not found on UPlight's own site or store (0 hits across 420 store listings and the maker's product sitemap, checked 2026-09-28). Modelled on the same class of 40 W RGB IP65 laser sold by other makers, e.g. Blue Sea's BLLO-RGB40.
items.identified: NOT FOUND — modelled on an EQUIVALENT
items.what: A sealed, waterproof box — not a moving head — that fires a laser beam out through a small window. Inside, a fast-steering mirror (a galvo) sweeps the beam to draw lines, fans, tunnels or full graphics in haze, or across an audience. It mixes red, green and blue diode lasers to draw in full colour.
items.inShow: Used for beam fans and tunnels over an audience, aerial 'gobos made of light', or fine graphic 'laser writing' — a different visual language from any LED fixture, and one a director may never have specified before.

needs.text: AC mains; about 1200 W drawn (includes cooling and electronics, not just the optical output).
Controlled by DMX, or by a laser-show interface/software (FB4, Pangolin Beyond).
Mounts on a stand or truss clamp; the IP65 body is rated for outdoor or damp use.

A laser of this power (tens of watts optical) is well above hand-held laser-pointer levels and falls under IEC 60825-1's higher hazard classes (3B/4). Before it is ever pointed at or over an audience it needs: a written laser safety assessment and an IEC 60825-1 classification of the actual unit; in the UK, compliance with the PLASA 'Guidance for the Safety of Display Lasers' that replaced HSE's HS(G)95; in the US, an FDA/CDRH variance from 21 CFR 1040.11(c) for any audience-scanning show. It should be operated only by a trained Laser Safety Officer (LSO), per ILDA's guidance.
A trained Laser Safety Officer (LSO) should run pre-show checks and hold responsibility for audience-scanning decisions.

20 W (half the power), IP65, cheaper — still a purpose-built show laser with DMX/Art-Net control.
